scenes.tts: A drug stops the cells making any new protein, and interferon still switches genes on. So the factor must already be in the cell. Two laboratories went looking, from opposite ends.

scenes.visual: A path in the middle of the frame: interferon on the left, three question-mark boxes, genes on the right. A drug strikes out new protein and the genes still turn green. Two arrows start from opposite ends; the one from the gene is named Darnell.
scenes.narration: A drug stops the cells making any new protein, and interferon still switches genes on. So the factor must already be in the cell. Two laboratories went looking, from opposite ends.

scenes.tts: James Darnell's laboratory started at the gene. It found a protein complex, I S G F 3, that binds a short DNA sequence shared by interferon-responsive genes. In August 1992, Christian Schindler, Ke Shuai and colleagues reported that interferon puts phosphate on its proteins' tyrosines. Staurosporine, a drug that blocks many kinases, stopped the activation. Some kinase had to act first. Which one, it could not say.

scenes.visual: DNA with a shared short sequence; ISGF3 proteins wait in the cytoplasm, interferon arrives, phosphate badges appear on tyrosine and the complex binds the sequence. Then staurosporine blocks it, nothing binds, and a question mark sits over the kinase.

scenes.tts: George Stark and Ian Kerr's laboratory started with genetics. Sandra Pellegrini built human cells with a marker gene controlled by interferon-responsive DNA. Only cells deaf to interferon survived. She screened about a hundred million mutagenized cells. Each mutant had lost a part of the pathway. She put DNA from normal cells into a mutant, and looked for the rare cell that recovered. In July 1992, her group in Paris reported the gene that rescued one mutant: T Y K 2.

scenes.visual: Cells carry DNA with a responsive stretch and a marker gene. Interferon is added and the responding cells fade, leaving a few deaf ones from a hundred million. A mutant has a missing part; normal DNA goes in and a rare cell recovers; the rescuing gene is TYK2.

scenes.tts: Two weeks apart, the results fit together. A JAK is required, and the DNA-binding proteins carry phosphotyrosine. Darnell's laboratory named those proteins STATs.

scenes.visual: A July and August 1992 timeline two weeks apart. The two arrows meet in the middle of the path: a JAK fills one question mark and the phosphotyrosine proteins fill the other, which are then labelled STATs.
